summary.title: Beautiful Code: A Regular Expression Matcher (Kernighan)
summary.one_liner: Learn how a compact, recursive C regular expression matcher of about 30 lines works, why its design is so small, and how to extend it.
takeaways: The matcher supports literal characters, '.', '^', '$', and '*' and fits in about 30 lines of C using recursion and pointer arithmetic.
match() tries each text position, while matchhere() and matchstar() handle the pattern one character at a time, recursing on the rest.
Backtracking makes patterns with several .* very slow, whereas an NFA-to-DFA approach as in egrep runs in time independent of the pattern.
Suggested extensions include +, ?, escaping, a compile phase, character classes, an opaque type, shell wildcards, a Java port, and wrapping Java's Pattern class.
summary.summary: This draft essay by Brian Kernighan describes the small regular expression matcher written by Rob Pike for The Practice of Programming, presented as an example of beautiful code. It gives the historical background of regular expressions in Ken Thompson's QED, ed, and grep, and explains why the pedagogical version focuses on grep-style features. The author walks through the C source for match, matchhere, and matchstar, covering termination conditions, shortest versus leftmost-longest matching, and performance compared with egrep. It closes with teaching exercises and reasons the code stays so compact.
